title: How to use a Q-Snap frame for cross-stitch
subtitle: Setting up and working with a rectangular plastic clip frame
excerpt: A Q-Snap frame is a plastic rectangular frame made from PVC pipes and clip-on sections. It holds the fabric taut without a hoop ring and causes no hoop marks or distortion on linen and fine evenweave. The clips release quickly and the fabric can be moved or re-tensioned at any stage of the project.
sourceNotes: Q-Snap frames are a contemporary cross-stitch accessory. Usage conventions described here follow standard needlework practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rectangular plastic frame made from PVC pipes and clip sections. Used as an alternative to a hoop for holding cross-stitch fabric taut. Leaves no hoop marks and suits large or stiff pieces.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: holds the fabric flat and even without pressing a rigid ring into the fibres the way a standard hoop does. The fabric slides over the PVC pipes and is then clipped in place by snap-on sections that compress the pipes and grip the fabric. The tension is even across the whole working area and there are no hoop marks to remove after washing.

Q-Snaps come in several standard sizes. The most common for cross-stitch are 11 x 11 cm, 17 x 17 cm, and 22 x 22 cm. For a piece wider than the frame, the frame clips only the section being worked at any time; the fabric is slid through the frame as the work advances. This makes Q-Snaps particularly useful for samplers and large landscape pieces.
Lay the fabric face-down over the base frame (the four PVC pipes without the clips attached). Centre the section you plan to work on over the frame.

Press each clip-on section over the corresponding pipe, trapping the fabric between the inner and outer pipe sections. Apply them one side at a time, pulling the fabric gently taut before clipping each side.
grid is square, not skewed. The holes should form straight rows in both directions. If the grid is diagonal, remove the clips, re-align the fabric, and re-clip.
Flip the frame over. The fabric is now face-up and the back of the piece is accessible between the pipes for thread management.

For a large piece, work the section of the design that is inside the frame, then release the clips, slide the fabric to expose the next section, and re-clip. Release the clips at the end of each session too, so the
that runs under the clips is not held under tension while stored. A thread under constant compression can weaken over weeks.

items.symptom: The fabric sags in the middle of the frame after a few minutes
items.cause: The clips were not snapped tightly enough, or the fabric was not pulled taut before the clips were applied.
items.fix: Remove the clips, re-tension the fabric with a gentle outward tug on each side, then snap the clips back on. If the fabric is too loose for the frame size, try a smaller frame.

items.symptom: The clips leave faint marks on the fabric
items.cause: The fabric was left in the frame under tension for an extended period.
items.fix: Release the clips at the end of each session. On linen, this is especially important as the fibres compress more readily than Aida.

content.text: Once the Q-Snap setup is comfortable, the next technique worth combining it with is gridding the fabric. A gridded piece in a Q-Snap frame is the standard setup for a long sampler project.
